lines.note: Souocu is a poorly built house, as explained by Voroſocana iye and the Portuguese. The unmarked o distinguishes this entry from the following grass-thatched dwelling.
The continuation adds that the house is poor or humble; it completes the preceding definition rather than forming a separate entry.
Sǒuocu is a house made of grass or similar vegetation. Cuſano iye supplies the Japanese paraphrase; the caron belongs to this headword, unlike Souocu above.
Choupana identifies the grass-built dwelling as a hut. This short, indented physical line completes the preceding explanation.

runs.text: Não ſe vſa aßi ſò ſe não com algũa cõ-

lines.note: Sǒuon is said not to be used by itself, only in a compound or expression. The Portuguese word for composition is divided after cõ- at the right edge.
Sandai sǒuonno qimi introduces a lord whose benefactions extend across three generations. The printed space after Sandai and the cedilla in poſição are retained; Se- begins senhor.

runs.text: nhor de quem ſe tem recebidos muitos beneficios

lines.note: The continuation identifies the lord as one from whom many benefits have been received. It carries the Portuguese explanation of the preceding Japanese expression.
The benefits extend back to the ancestors. The printed separation ante paßados is preserved rather than modernizing the Portuguese compound.
Sôxa denotes an intermediary who speaks or conveys messages for others. Mǒxitçugui and toritçuguite are alternative Japanese explanations, not terms embedded in Portuguese prose.

runs.text: mem que tem por officio falar por outros, ou

lines.note: The intermediary has the duty of speaking on behalf of others. The alternative duty introduced by ou continues onto the next physical line.
Carrying messages to the lord completes the duties of the sôxa. The final senhor belongs to this definition, not the following place-name.

runs.text: Lugar como portaria onde ſe to-

lines.note: Sôxadocoro is the place where such messages are received, compared with a porter’s lodge or reception office. To- is the printed beginning of tomão.
The continuation completes tomão os recados, receiving messages. The historical nasal ending is preserved as printed.

runs.text: Sǒxei. Youo fayǒ ſu. i, Youo fayǒ ſaru.

lines.note: The entry concerns leaving life early: Youo fayǒ ſu is explained by Youo fayǒ ſaru. The damaged headword is read Sǒxei, supported by the supplied NINJAL index; its first vowel and accent are weak in this impression.

runs.text: morrer de pouca idade, ou de preßa.

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies dying young or quickly, confirming the early-death sense rather than resurrection in the next entry.
Soxei is resurrection or revival, paraphrased by Yomigayeru. Its unmarked vowel is retained independently of the previous headword.
Soxei xita fito means a person who has come back to life. The Portuguese past-tense verb confirms that the example describes the revived person.
Sǒxen, explained by Auoi coqe, denotes green moss. The initial is S, not OCR B; the terminal written-register label is a separate upright S., with no following lexical a.
Soxet is white snow, with Xirayuqi as its Japanese explanation. The final t is retained as the historical checked-syllable spelling.
Sǒxet combines frost and snow, explicitly paired as Ximo, yuqi. The caron distinguishes this compound from the preceding snow entry.
Soxi refers to eminent ancient founders. The Portuguese relative clause continues below to identify the religious traditions they founded.
The founders established a religion or sect. Soxi xento- continues as xentocu below; the damaged t is read from its surviving foot and the meaningful compound, not as OCR e.
Cu completes xentocu, paired with Soxi for ancestral founders and earlier worthies. Idem refers to the same definition and is not a new headword.
Sǒxi names books of verse or narrative. Narabu cami explains their assembled sheets; hi- begins the Portuguese word for histories or stories.

runs.text: ſtorias eſcritos em lingua branda de Iapão.

lines.note: The books are written in the vernacular or plain language of Japan. The damaged country-name is read Iapão; its descender and the bilingual context exclude the OCR laſão.
Here Sǒxi means three or four. Sǒxinin tçurete begins an example about taking three or four companions; the initial Portuguese word is Tres, not OCR Pres.
The example continues with dressing more carefully than usual and going out. Feiq. is the upright citation label, separate from the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Lib. 10. Leuando conſigo em companhia tres,

lines.note: The printed reference is Lib. 10. The Portuguese translation begins by describing the three or four accompanying people; the line ends with a comma.

runs.text: ou quatro homens, ſahio milhor atauiado, &

lines.note: The person went out better dressed than usual. ſahio, meaning went out, replaces OCR ſabio and agrees with iderareta in the Japanese example.
The first example concludes with being more splendidly dressed than usual. Cami sǒ xi- begins the second example, counting three or four sheets of paper.

runs.text: Tres, ou quatro folhas de papel.

lines.note: Mai completes the paper-counter example, translated as three or four sheets. It is the continuation of xi-mai, not an independent entry.

runs.text: Filhos de pois do morgado, ou qualquer

lines.note: Soxi denotes sons other than the primary heir. The initial S is damaged but identifiable; reading Foxi would disconnect the headword from this definition.
The continuation clarifies that any son who is not the heir is included. Morgado is the Portuguese inheritance term used by the dictionary.
Sǒxi here means a brief interval. Sǒxi tenpai supplies a synonymous expression, distinct from the preceding numerical and kinship entries.

runs.text: O meſmo. i, em quanto hum leuanta a cabeça

lines.note: The brief interval is explained as the time taken to raise one’s head. The explanatory clause continues on the next row.
Raising or lowering the head completes the illustration of a momentary interval. The printed alternatives are preserved without combining physical lines.
Sôxi and its principal forms mean addressing the ruler. Quan- begins the following musical-performance example.
Quanguenuo sǒſuru means performing instrumental music before the ruler. The example visibly has a caron in sǒſuru; it is not normalized to the headword’s circumflex.
The musical gloss ends with performance before the ruler. Bugacu and the divided cagura introduce the next example of music and dance.
Gurauo completes cagurauo, followed by ſôſuru. The Portuguese describes singing and dancing; di- continues diante on the next row.

runs.text: ante do Rey, ou do Cami.

lines.note: The performance takes place before the ruler or a kami. Cami occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is therefore recorded as a whole-word typeface target.
Sǒxiguiri is an awl used in closing letters. The Portuguese verb is fechar, with f, rather than the OCR’s ſechar.
Soxin is explained by Voroſocana cocoro, a neglectful or indifferent heart. The Japanese adjective’s ſo sequence replaces the malformed OCR bc.
The heart is described as unloving or careless. The upright S. is the written-register label, not part of the italic definition.
Sôxin denotes being destroyed or brought to an end. The repeated Sôxin begins a longer expression explained through exhausting hardship.

The expression begun with Sôxin is completed by xumiǒ, whose dotted i follows m on renewed inspection. It describes dying under hardships and afflictions; the accent area of mortò is stained, so the baseline grave is retained provisionally.

runs.text: çoẽs, como os que por amor de Deos, ou da

lines.note: Çoẽs completes afliçoẽs. The example concerns enduring hardship for love of God or another purpose, and continues at the top of the second column.

runs.text: ſaluação, ou deſeu ſenhor, &c. não tem dó

lines.note: The cross-column continuation adds salvation or service to one’s lord as motives. Não tem dó begins the statement that such people do not spare their own lives.

runs.text: da vida, nem perdoão a trabalhos, &c.

lines.note: The sentence concludes that they spare neither life nor labour. This belongs to Sôxin, before the independent Sǒxinen entry.
Sǒxinen means three or four years, extending the numerical Sǒxi expression found in the first column.
Soxiri is the noun for disparagement or murmuring against someone. The following entry supplies the corresponding verb forms.
The verb Soxiri, ru, xitta means to disparage or revile. The printed ru is retained, rather than regularizing the principal-form notation.

runs.text: Soxij. Arai xocu. i, Varui cuimono.

lines.note: Soxij is paraphrased as rough food or bad provisions by Arai xocu and Varui cuimono. Co- begins the Portuguese Comer on the next line.
Mer completes Comer, qualified as coarse and poor. The line completes the food gloss rather than introducing an action example.

runs.text: Pedir algũa couſa a peßoa alta. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Soxô means petitioning a person of high rank. The terminal vowel bears a circumflex; Item introduces a second sense below.
The second sense is accusing someone. Soxô ſuru gives the verbal expression, following italic Vt.
Sôxǒ denotes the leading master of linked-verse poets. Rengano xixǒ is the Japanese explanation; the Portuguese description continues below.

runs.text: dos poetas que cõpoem juntos huns verſos que

lines.note: The poets compose verses jointly. The nasal abbreviation in cõpoem is retained, and the explanation continues into the name of the verse form.
The jointly composed verses are called Renga. This is a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese prose, and its upright type is distinguished from the surrounding gloss.
Sôxocu is the colour of grass or herbs, explained by Cuſano iro. The upright S. marks written usage.
Soxocu denotes coarse food, with Voroſocana xocubut as the Japanese explanation. The scan reads Comer groſ-, not the OCR Comter greſ-.
The divided adjective finishes as groſſeiro, followed by ruim, poor or bad. This continues the food definition.

runs.text: O que pede, ou propoem ao ſenhor

lines.note: Soxônin is a petitioner who makes a request or proposal to the lord. The object of that request follows on the next line.
Algũa couſa completes the petitioner’s request for something. The physical continuation remains separate despite its short length.
Sǒxǔ is early autumn, paraphrased by Fayaqi aqi. The final q with a tilde abbreviates the relative word introducing the calendar explanation.

runs.text: he na ſeptima lũa, ou mes.

lines.note: The dictionary locates early autumn in the seventh lunar month. ſeptima is a single printed word, not OCR ſe ptima.
Sôxu collectively denotes Buddhist monks, explained by Bozutachi and Portuguese Bonzos. No long-vowel mark is supplied to Bozutachi.

runs.text: Conſulta, ou parecer de todos em v-

lines.note: Sôxugui means consultation or the opinion of everyone collectively. The final v- begins vniuerſal on the following row.
Sôxuguini itasǒ means acting according to the collective view. Farei begins the Portuguese first-person translation.
The translation concludes that the speaker will follow everyone’s opinion. The damaged final word is todos, not OCR nocos.
Soxxi and its principal forms mean gathering people. Xei- begins the object of the illustrative expression.
The continuation forms Xeiuo ſoſſuru, gathering a force or people. Both medial long-s types are visible, restoring the consonant omitted by OCR.

runs.text: Frechas que tem o ferro redondo, & a-

lines.note: Soya denotes arrows whose iron heads are rounded in section. The final a- begins the description of their sharp tips.
Gudo completes agudo: the arrowhead is sharp at the point. This qualifies the preceding rounded-head description.
Sôyacunin is a chief official or steward. The damaged y belongs to a single headword, not the OCR punctuation and separated acunin.
Principal completes the description of the senior steward or overseer. It is body text continuing the same entry.
Soyaxi means provoking or persuading someone, with the objectionable object specified below. Prouocar has u, not OCR n.

runs.text: alguem algũa couſa que não conuem.

lines.note: The persuasion concerns something inappropriate or inadvisable. This completes the negative sense of Soyaxi rather than a neutral request.
Soyaxitate has the same meaning as Soyaxi. The printed principal forms tçuru and eta are preserved without modernizing their notation.
Sǒye is clothing made from plant fibres, explained by Cuſano coromo. The worn headword is distinguished from the unaccented verb Soye below; li- begins linho.
The materials include hemp linen and cotton. Sǒ- begins the repeated headword in the expression continued on the next row.

Sǒye mocujiqi combines coarse clothing with eating tree fruits. The damaged Portuguese vowel is read o; the aligned baseline’s single long ſ is retained in groſeiro because a possible second stroke is not secure.
The food consists of the fruits of trees. This completes mocujiqi in the preceding expression, not a botanical identification.
Soye and its principal forms mean adding something. Coco- begins cocorouo in the illustrative expression below.
Cocorouo ſoyuru is explained as helping or favouring someone. It is an idiomatic extension of adding one’s attention or support.
Cotobauo ſoyuru means adding verbal support, translated as helping with words. The damaged t and b replace OCR Conobauo.

runs.text: Couſa que ſe acrecenta como nas compras,

lines.note: The noun Soye is an addition or extra, illustrated through buying and selling. The explanation continues across the next line.

runs.text: & vendas, ou q̃ ſe da alem do que ſe vende.

lines.note: The extra may be given beyond what is sold. The opening sign is an ampersand linking purchases and sales, not OCR co.
Soyeuo ſuru provides the verb phrase for making or giving the addition. Italic Vt introduces the Japanese example.
Soyego is a small knife or penknife. The two Portuguese alternatives are preserved without assigning a more specific implement.

runs.text: Soar o vento por cima das ar-

lines.note: Soyemeqi describes the sound of wind over vegetation. The printed abbreviated principal form u is retained; ar- begins aruores.
The wind passes over trees or herbs, completing the sound description. The two plant categories remain the dictionary’s own broad terms.

runs.text: Soyen. Voroſoca touoxi. i, Fitono nacano

lines.note: Soyen denotes distant or estranged relations. Voroſoca touoxi supplies a Japanese paraphrase, and Fitono nacano begins the further explanation.
Vtoutoxiqi describes estrangement between people, replacing the garbled OCR icutoaiqi. The Portuguese sem ſe- continues with ver at the next page’s opening; the separate bottom ver is a catchword.

zones.label: Column 2 catchword
zones.note: Repeats the opening word on bnf-f0451; not an additional body line.
